newsitem.title: GABON: Two wounded in Gabon poll clash.
newsitem.headline: Two wounded in Gabon poll clash.

text.p: Two people suffered gunshot wounds in northern Gabon on Sunday in a clash during the second round of the Central African nation's parliamentary election, an electoral official said.
President Omar Bongo's party looked on course for a comfortable majority over the opposition. Less than half the national assembly's 120 seats were decided in the first round vote on December 15.
Rivalry among Bongo's own supporters has been intense, with many ruling Democratic Party members standing as independents after failing to win the party ticket.
The clash took place in the town of Bitam near the border with Cameroon, where two members of Bongo's party were contesting the seat, one standing as an independent.
Polling resumed later and electoral officials said that apart from the clash and a couple of lesser incidents, voting in other areas passed off peacefully.
The elections are part of a democratic timetable brokered in Paris in 1994 after political violence shook the oil-producing Central African nation, killing more than a dozen people.
Bongo's party won 47 of the 55 seats decided on December 15.
The main opposition National Woodcutters Rally (RNB), who won control of Libreville in chaotic October municipal elections, won three seats on December 15.
They and other opposition parties have called for the parliamentary elections to be rerun, denouncing problems with voter cards and electoral lists during the first round.
Witnesses said polling was calm for the one seat still to be decided in the capital Libreville on Sunday.

Poll officials said an election official was attacked at Onga in the southeast and ballot boxes smashed in the southern town of Moabi, where the Woodcutters' number two, Pierre Andre Kombila, faced a ruling party candidate.
The elections are Gabon's second multiparty legislative polls. The first were in 1990 when a wave of democratic reform swept across Africa after the fall of Soviet-bloc communism.
Bongo has ruled the former French colony since 1968 after the death of Gabon's founding head of state, Leon Mba. His presidential term ends in 1998.
